title: But how do AI images and videos actually work? (Welch Labs / 3Blue1Brown)

scenes.title: Scene 1 · The Generative Revolution
scenes.narration: Over the last few years, AI systems have become astonishingly good at turning text prompts into videos.

scenes.title: Scene 2 · Brownian Motion & Reverse Entropy
scenes.narration: At the core of how these models operate is a deep connection to physics. This generation of image and video models works using a process known as diffusion, which is remarkably equivalent to the Brownian motion we see as particles diffuse, but with time run backwards, and in high-dimensional space.

motion_cues.description: Camera dollies forward into microscopic Brownian fluid simulation
Luminescent dye particles diffuse outward in stochastic random walks
Velocity vectors attach to each particle showing instantaneous momentum
Vectors flip 180 degrees: noise particles coalesce back into structured form

scenes.title: Scene 3 · Density Manifolds & The Score Function
scenes.narration: As we'll see, this connection to physics is much more than a curiosity. We get real algorithms out of the physics that we can use to generate images and videos. And this perspective will also give us some really nice intuitions for how these models work in practice.
scenes.display_formula: s_θ(x_t, t) ≈ ∇_{x_t} log p_t(x_t)  [Score Function Field]

scenes.title: Scene 4 · Hands-On with WAN 2.1 & Prompt Steering
scenes.narration: But before we dive into this connection, let's get hands-on with a real diffusion model. While the best models are closed source, there are some compelling open source models. This video of an astronaut was generated by an open source model called WAN 2.1. We can add to our prompt and have our astronaut hold a flag, hold a laptop, or hold a meeting.

WAN 2.1 photorealistic astronaut video plays in cinema viewport
Prompt chips dynamically cycle: [hold a flag] -> [hold a laptop] -> [hold a meeting]
